name: Compatibilism
statement: Free will and determinism can both be true: you can act freely even if your choice was caused.
statementAccent: you can act freely even if your choice was caused
meaning: Compatibilism is the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism, that a person can act freely, and be morally responsible, even if determinism is true and their actions are causally necessitated by prior events and the laws of nature. It is opposed to incompatibilism, on which free will and determinism cannot both hold. Compatibilism has taken several forms. Classical compatibilism, associated with Hobbes, Hume, Mill, and later Schlick and Ayer, analyzes free action as acting according to one's own will and desires, without external constraint, coercion, or impediment; freedom is the absence of obstacles, doing what one wants. Hume characterized liberty as a power of acting or not acting according to the determinations of the will, a hypothetical liberty, and classical compatibilists offered a conditional analysis of the ability to do otherwise, on which one could have done otherwise means one would have done otherwise if one had chosen or wanted to. Contemporary compatibilism refines this. Harry Frankfurt's hierarchical, or mesh, theory locates free will in a harmony between one's effective first-order desires and one's second-order volitions, so that one acts freely when one has the will one wants. John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza's reasons-responsiveness view, a semicompatibilism, grounds responsibility in guidance control exercised through the agent's own moderately reasons-responsive mechanism. P. F. Strawson grounded responsibility in the reactive attitudes. Compatibilism has been the majority view among philosophers and is sometimes called soft determinism.
mechanism: Compatibilism defuses the apparent conflict between free will and determinism by identifying the freedom relevant to responsibility with something a determined agent can possess. Classical compatibilists argue that what matters for free action is not whether one's choice was ultimately caused but whether it flowed from one's own will without external interference: an agent who does what they want, unconstrained and uncoerced, acts freely even if their wanting was itself determined. On this view the worry that a determined agent could not have done otherwise is met by a conditional analysis: to say one could have done otherwise is to say that one would have done otherwise had one chosen or wanted to, and this conditional can be true in a deterministic world. Contemporary compatibilists deepen the account by asking not just whether an action flows from the agent's desires but whether it flows from them in the right way. Frankfurt distinguishes first-order desires, to do this or that, from second-order volitions, desires about which desire moves one to act, and holds that one has free will when one's effective desire is the one endorsed at the higher level, as the willing addict has and the unwilling addict lacks. Fischer and Ravizza shift the focus from the ability to do otherwise, regulative control, to guidance control, the actual-sequence capacity to act on a mechanism that is the agent's own and is moderately responsive to reasons, arguing that responsibility requires this even if determinism rules out alternative possibilities, a position they call semicompatibilism. P. F. Strawson takes a different route, arguing that our practices of holding responsible rest on the reactive attitudes, such as resentment and gratitude, which are not undermined by the abstract truth of determinism.

examples.text: Classical compatibilists count an act free when it flows from one's own desires without external constraint or coercion.
One acts freely, on Frankfurt's view, when one's effective desire is the one endorsed by one's higher-order volitions.
Fischer and Ravizza ground responsibility in guidance control through the agent's own moderately reasons-responsive mechanism.

variants.name: Classical compatibilism
variants.text: Freedom as acting on one's desires without external constraint, with a conditional analysis of the ability to do otherwise.

variants.name: Semicompatibilism
variants.text: Fischer and Ravizza's view that moral responsibility is compatible with determinism even if the freedom to do otherwise is not.

whyItMatters: Compatibilism is the most widely held position in the free will debate and offers the most influential attempt to reconcile our sense of ourselves as responsible agents with the possibility that the world is deterministic. Its importance lies in showing that the threat determinism seems to pose to freedom may rest on a confusion, by distinguishing the freedom that matters for responsibility, acting from one's own will, or through a reasons-responsive mechanism that is one's own, from a more metaphysically demanding freedom that a determined agent could not have. This move lets compatibilists preserve the practices of praise, blame, and desert without betting on the falsity of determinism or on libertarian indeterminism. The tradition runs from Hobbes and Hume through Mill to a rich contemporary literature, and it has produced landmark contributions: Frankfurt's hierarchical theory and his cases against the requirement of alternative possibilities, Fischer and Ravizza's semicompatibilist account of guidance control, and P. F. Strawson's reorientation of the whole debate toward the reactive attitudes that structure human relationships. Whether or not one accepts it, compatibilism sets much of the agenda for thinking about freedom and responsibility. As the view that free will and determinism can coexist, it is a central position in metaphysics and ethics.

working.text: identify free will with acting from one's own will, not with escaping causal determination.

add higher-order endorsement or reasons-responsiveness so the action flows from the agent in the right way.

limits: Compatibilism faces persistent objections, above all that it changes the subject. Incompatibilists charge that classical compatibilism secures only freedom of action, the absence of external constraint, while leaving untouched the deeper worry that a determined agent's very desires and will are themselves the products of causes reaching back before their birth, so that the agent is not the ultimate source of what they do. The conditional analysis of the ability to do otherwise is widely thought to fail, since an agent might satisfy the conditional yet, being determined, still not be genuinely able to choose otherwise, and the analysis threatens a regress into could have chosen otherwise. Manipulation and covert-control arguments press that an agent secretly engineered to have exactly the mesh or reasons-responsiveness the compatibilist requires seems unfree in just the way a determined agent is feared to be, suggesting the compatibilist conditions are not enough. Higher-order theories face a regress about what authorizes the higher-order desire. Some details reward care: soft determinism is William James's term and applies only to compatibilists who are also determinists, and certain datings and quotations are best drawn from the primary texts. So compatibilism robustly reconciles freedom with determinism, understood as a leading but contested position challenged by the sourcehood worry, the failure of the conditional analysis, and manipulation arguments.
misreadings: Compatibilism does not assert that determinism is true, only that free will would be compatible with it; a compatibilist may think the world indeterministic. It is not the claim that we are free from causal influence, but that the freedom that matters is a matter of how our actions are caused, not whether. And soft determinism is not a synonym for compatibilism in general, since it names specifically the compatibilist who is also a determinist, so treating compatibilism as asserting determinism, as denying causation of choices, or as identical to soft determinism, misreads the view.
origin: The thesis, defended from Hobbes and Hume through Frankfurt, Fischer and Ravizza, and P. F. Strawson, that free will and moral responsibility are compatible with determinism, opposed to incompatibilism.
